papers.title: Stinespring's Dilation, Universal-NOT, and Limitations of Quantum Uncoupled Learning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27251v1

summary.one_liner: The paper shows that quantum versions of uncoupled learning dynamics (players who see only their own payoff and update quantum strategy states through physically valid channels) cannot reach Nash equilibrium in certain conjugation games without some memory, and characterizes when small classical or quantum memory helps.
summary.plain: The paper studies how two players, each choosing a quantum state as their strategy, can learn toward a stable outcome when each only sees the other's current state and their own payoff. It shows that in a specific family of games, a memoryless update rule that must be physically realizable cannot make the learner reach the equilibrium. It also shows that a small amount of classical memory fixes this for any finite set of target strategies, but no finite memory suffices for all possible pure qubit targets.
summary.why: It identifies a concrete case where the physical requirement that quantum updates be realizable, not just the lack of information, blocks learning, which matters for decentralized learning in quantum systems. The text does not show links to specific applications, so the broader significance is uncertain.
summary.background:
- Nash equilibrium: a set of strategies where no player gains by changing alone.
- Uncoupled learning: each player updates using only their own payoff, not the opponent's full strategy or payoffs.
- Qubit: the quantum analogue of a bit; a pure qubit state is a point on a sphere of possible states.
- Quantum channel: a physically allowed way to transform a quantum state (it must be consistent with quantum mechanics).
- Stinespring's dilation theorem: a result stating that any physical channel can be realized by adding an environment and applying a unitary (reversible) operation.
- Universal-NOT: an operation that tries to flip an unknown quantum state; its best achievable accuracy is limited by quantum mechanics (the Bužek, Hillery, Werner bound).
- Conjugation game: a game where the best response for one player is the transpose of the other's strategy.

papers.abstract: Uncoupled learning, in which players know only their own payoff, are a standard model of decentralized learning toward Nash equilibrium. We study their quantum counterpart, where strategies are quantum states and, in each round, a player receives a physical copy of their opponent's current strategy and updates their own state by a quantum channel. This adds to uncoupledness a constraint with no classical analogue: every update must be physically realizable. In fact, this constraint is decisive in conjugation games, in which Bob has a strictly dominant pure strategy and Alice's unique best response is its transpose. In this work, we show some limitations of uncoupled (learning) dynamics in finding the Nash equilibrium for conjugation games. First, we prove that no autonomous, memoryless, uncoupled dynamics converge to Nash equilibrium in a family of four single-qubit conjugation games. Specifically, any memoryless channel that keeps all four equilibria fixed will leave Alice's strategy frozen. This result also extends to $4^n$ games on $n$-qubit registers. Second, we show that this barrier disappears with a small classical memory: for any finite family of $L$ pure targets, a guess-and-test rule with $O(\log L)$ classical bits converges to equilibrium, with an explicit bound on its convergence rate. Finally, we prove that no finite memory, classical or quantum, suffices for the continuum of all pure-qubit targets. Our proof of the impossibility for memoryless channels relies on Stinespring's dilation theorem, while the impossibility for finite-memory channels relies on the optimal universal-NOT (in)fidelity bound by Bu\v{z}ek, Hillery, and Werner.

papers.title: Learning under Bounded Manipulation for Quadratic Incentive Design
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26736v1

summary.one_liner: A repeated quadratic incentive design game in which a leader estimates a follower's private type from noisy actions while the follower strategically deviates to manipulate those estimates, with a minimax regret bound of order max{log T, min{C_T, T}} under a manipulation budget C_T.
summary.plain: A "leader" (for example, a principal setting pay or rewards) tries to learn something private about a "follower" (an agent) by watching what the follower does, then sets incentives based on that guess. The follower knows how the leader learns, so he can act slightly differently from his best short-term choice to steer what the leader concludes later. The paper measures how much this manipulation costs the leader and shows how that cost scales with how much the follower is allowed to manipulate.
summary.why: It addresses a practical concern in learning-based incentive design: an agent who knows the learning rule can game it, so a learner's performance depends on the agent's strategic ability and not only on noise. The text does not say how it relates to specific applications, so its wider significance beyond this model is unclear.
summary.background:
- Incentive design (Stackelberg-style game): a leader commits to a rule, and a follower responds to maximize his own payoff.
- Quadratic/affine incentive rule: the leader's payment is a linear function of the follower's action, with the leader's estimate of the follower's type as a parameter.
- Regret: how much worse a learner does compared with an oracle that knows the true private type from the start; minimax regret is the best worst-case guarantee over all policies.
- Manipulation budget C_T: a cap on the total squared deviation the follower may add over T rounds, beyond his myopic best response.
- Log T rate: the usual slow growth of error for learning from noisy data; the extra term shows the cost of manipulation.
- Information-theoretic lower bound: a limit that holds for any policy, no matter how clever, given the information available.

papers.abstract: We study a repeated quadratic incentive design game in which a leader learns a follower's private type from noisy observations of the follower's actions and uses her estimates in an affine incentive rule. The follower knows the leader's learning policy, which incorporates past observations to produce estimates of the follower's type, and can deviate from his myopic best response to influence the leader's future estimates. We ask how the follower's ability to manipulate these observations affects the leader's performance. Under a manipulation budget $C_T$ constraining the expected cumulative squared deviation of the follower's actions from his myopic best response, we establish a minimax regret rate of order $\max\{\log T, \min\{C_T,T\}\}$ for approximately rational followers. Our information-theoretic lower bound applies to a general class of causal estimation and manipulation policies for the leader and the follower. We provide a simple learning policy that achieves the lower bound. Finally, we show that under a fixed learning rule, increasing the manipulation budget of the follower can counterintuitively reduce the leader's regret.

papers.title: Bottlenecked: The Capital Cost of Protected DeFi Lending
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26948v1

summary.background:
- DeFi: lending and borrowing run by smart contracts on public blockchains, without a traditional bank.
- Collateral: assets locked up to secure a loan.
- Composability: protocols can be stacked, so one protocol's assets can be reused as collateral in another, letting a single exploit spread.
- Junior capital: a first-loss buffer that absorbs losses before senior creditors (here, users) are hit; similar to a deductible or insurance layer.
- Tripartite graph: a three-part network linking user assets, the liabilities they cover, and the junior capital available to pay them.
- Static security game: a game-theory model in which an attacker picks a strategy against fixed defenses, used here to price the protection.
- Θ(N) vs Θ(√N): asymptotic growth rates; as the number of borrowers N grows, the optimized design's insurance cost grows much more slowly.
- Kelp exploit (April 2026): an attack, cited in the paper, in which roughly $300 million in stolen bridged assets was used as borrowed collateral across lending markets.
summary.one_liner: The paper models how junior (first-loss) capital should be allocated across a tripartite graph of user assets, covered liabilities, and protecting capital in DeFi lending, defines an adversarial default premium via a static security game, and shows an optimized graph can scale insurance cost as Θ(√N) versus Θ(N) for Aave- and Morpho-like designs.
summary.plain: Decentralized lending protocols hold large sums, and when hackers exploit them, losses can spread across linked lending markets. This paper asks how much backup money (a first layer of capital that takes losses before users do) such systems need, and where it should be placed. The authors model this as a network diagram, define a cost for the protection, and report that an optimized layout could cut the capital cost by up to 34.5% compared with designs resembling Aave and Morpho, based on estimates applied to 2026 attacks.
summary.why: Losses from DeFi exploits are large and can cascade through composable protocols, so how much capital to hold and where is a practical design question. The idea of treating junior capital as a core design constraint may be useful for protocol designers, though the results rest on the authors' model and assumptions, which the summary text does not fully spell out.

papers.abstract: Securing hundreds of billions of dollars in decentralized finance (DeFi) requires both cryptographically secured collateral and economic capital to absorb losses that collateral alone cannot cover. Composability makes both the amount and location of this protection matter: Kelp's nearly \$300 million April 2026 bridge exploit showed how an attacker could borrow against stolen assets across lending markets. We study how to allocate junior capital that absorbs losses before users incur losses in lending protocols. The main object we study is a tripartite graph that records user assets, their covered liabilities, and the junior capital permitted to pay them. Cuts in this graph determine what protection is missing, while a static security game on the graph defines how much such protection should cost. We call this cost the adversarial default premium (ADP), which can be viewed as the excess cost of insurance in composable financial systems. We then study the joint cost of funding loans and protecting their creditors via this insurance. In a tripartite graph with $N$ borrowers and $M$ lenders, we show that existing systems such as Aave and Morpho have an insurance cost that is $Θ(N)$. Under mild assumptions, we show that the optimal graph has an insurance cost that is $Θ(\sqrt{N})$ with small constants. We apply our model to numerous 2026 DeFi cyber attacks and estimate ADP and the performance of optimized graphs. We find practical capital cost savings of up to 34.5% for our optimized design versus designs that resemble Aave and Morpho. Our results suggest that new lending protocols can improve capital efficiency by treating junior capital as a first-class constraint in protocol design.

papers.title: Uniqueness, Proximity, and Scaling in Atomic Splittable Polymatroid Congestion Games
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25757v1

summary.background:
- Congestion game: players choose resources; each resource's cost rises with the number of users.
- Equilibrium: a split where no player can lower its own cost by changing its choice alone.
- Splittable demand: a player can divide its demand across several resources rather than picking one.
- Atomic: each player is a single, non-negligible participant, not a tiny crowd member.
- Polymatroid: a combinatorial structure generalizing capacity limits on sets of resources, defined by a rank function.
- Affine latency: a cost that rises linearly with load (a constant plus slope times load); positive slope means cost increases with load.
- Submodular function minimization: a standard polynomial-time optimization tool over these structures.
- Polynomial time: the running time grows at most as a polynomial in the input size.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives a polynomial-time exact algorithm for equilibria in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games with affine latencies, via integer-packet approximations and proximity arguments built on an Oki–Schwarcz multiple-exchange theorem, and proves equilibrium uniqueness for arbitrary real polymatroid ranks with convex, strictly increasing latencies.
summary.plain: The paper studies a model where several players share a network of resources and each splits its demand across them, with congestion making each resource slower as more load lands on it. The authors show how to compute the stable split (the equilibrium) exactly and efficiently, by first solving a version where demand moves in fixed-size chunks and then shrinking the chunks step by step. They also prove that, under broad conditions, this stable state is the only one.
summary.why: Equilibrium computation in congestion-type games matters for traffic, network routing, and resource sharing, where it is useful to know both that a stable outcome can be found and that it is unique. The uniqueness result is stated as resolving a previously open problem, though the text alone does not show how widely that problem was discussed. Connections beyond this specialist setting are not established in the text.

papers.abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games with integral ranks and rational player-specific affine latencies with positive slopes. The algorithm first computes equilibria of associated integer-splittable games, in which demands are allocated in multiples of a common packet size. For arbitrary polymatroid bases, no polynomial-time algorithm for these discrete equilibria was previously known. We provide such an algorithm and use progressively finer packets to recover the continuous equilibrium exactly. Our proof uses the multiple-exchange theorem of Oki and Schwarcz (2025) to obtain two exchange matchings that yield equilibrium proximity under changes of packet sizes and ranks, independently of cost coefficients. We then bound the matching deficiency caused by rank changes and construct compatible submodular rank roundings. Together these give a polynomial-time packet-halving algorithm using polynomially many submodular-function minimizations and exact rational arithmetic. The analysis rests on a uniqueness theorem of independent interest: for arbitrary real polymatroid ranks and continuously differentiable, strictly increasing, convex latencies, we prove uniqueness of equilibria, resolving a previously open problem.

papers.title: Closing Gaps in Temporal Fair Division for Chores
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25892v1

summary.background:
- Indivisible chores: tasks that cannot be split and that each agent dislikes doing (each has a cost to each agent).
- Envy-freeness up to one chore (EF1): no agent would prefer another's bundle after removing one task from that bundle.
- Temporal fairness: the fairness condition must hold after every prefix of arrivals, not just at the end, and assignments are fixed once made.
- NP-hardness / NP-completeness: a standard notion from computational complexity meaning no known efficient algorithm is expected; "unless P = NP" is the usual caveat.
- Approximation and FPTAS: an algorithm that gets within a guaranteed factor of the best answer; an FPTAS does so in time polynomial in the input and in 1/error for fixed parameters.
- Social cost: the total cost all agents incur under an allocation.
summary.one_liner: The paper settles open questions on temporal EF1 fairness for indivisible chores: it shows such allocations need not exist for three or more agents, that deciding their existence is NP-complete, and that minimizing social cost under TEF1 is hard to approximate, while an FPTAS exists for the optimal temporal EF1 factor.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to split up unpleasant tasks (chores) among several people when the tasks arrive in a fixed order and cannot be reassigned. It asks whether a split exists where nobody ever feels they have a clearly worse share, up to the removal of one task, at every point in time. The authors show that for three or more people such splits sometimes do not exist, that checking whether one exists is computationally hard, and how this interacts with the total cost of the tasks.
summary.why: This settles a question that an earlier paper left open and conjectured, so it matters for anyone designing fair task-sharing rules over time. The link to social cost is a concrete trade-off: a small loosening of the fairness requirement permits efficient computation, which may be relevant to practical scheduling or allocation systems, though the text itself does not discuss applications.

papers.abstract: We study the fair division of indivisible chores that must be assigned in a prescribed order. The complete instance is known in advance, but assignments cannot be changed. Temporal envy-freeness up to one chore (TEF1) requires envy-freeness up to one chore after every arrival. For goods, TEF1 allocations need not exist, and deciding whether one exists is NP-hard. For chores, Elkind et al. (AAMAS 2025) showed that TEF1 allocations exist for two agents, but left open whether they always exist, conjecturing that they do not, and whether deciding their existence is hard. We resolve both questions, confirming the conjecture in a strong form: for every $n\ge3$ and every finite factor, some $n$-agent instance admits no allocation satisfying TEF1 even up to that factor. This holds even when all agents have the same multiset of individual chore costs, with nine chores sufficing for three agents. Deciding TEF1 existence is NP-complete for every fixed $n\ge3$, even when all costs lie within a factor $1+2^{-m}$ of one another, where $m$ is the number of chores. Instances without TEF1 allocations exist arbitrarily close to the uniform cost matrix with $O(n\log n)$ chores, and just nineteen for three agents. We then relate fairness to social cost. Even when a TEF1 allocation is supplied, minimizing social cost subject to TEF1 admits no polynomial-time approximation within any factor polynomial in the number of chores unless P$=$NP, already for three agents with strictly positive normalized costs. In contrast, for every fixed number of agents, we give an FPTAS for the optimal temporal EF1 factor, the smallest factor up to which TEF1 can be satisfied, whose output has social cost no larger than that of the cheapest allocation attaining this factor. Thus a slight relaxation of fairness permits a social-cost guarantee that, unless P$=$NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can provide under exact TEF1.

papers.title: Temporal Fair Division: Simultaneous Guarantees for Goods and Chores
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23782v1

summary.background:
- Fair division: splitting indivisible items among agents so that each feels treated fairly.
- Goods vs. chores: goods are things agents like to receive; chores are costs agents want to minimize.
- Temporal setting: items arrive one by one in a known order and each must be assigned immediately and permanently.
- Proportionality up to one item (PROP1): each agent gets at least their fair share, up to a single item's margin.
- Maximin share (MMS): the best guaranteed share an agent could secure by splitting items into groups themselves; a 'temporal' version requires this at every step.
- Envy-freeness up to one item (EF1): no agent prefers another's bundle after removing one item from it.
- Approximation factor: a multiplier showing how close a guarantee comes to the ideal; 1/n and 2-1/n are such factors.
- Scheduling lower bounds: known limits from job scheduling that transfer to this problem.
summary.one_liner: Online-style fair division of indivisible goods and chores where items arrive over time and must be assigned irrevocably, giving algorithms that simultaneously meet several temporal fairness notions (TPROP1, TMMS, TEF1) with tight approximation factors for chores.
summary.plain: This paper studies how to split a stream of items among several people when each item must be handed out right away and cannot be taken back, and the split has to look fair after every new item arrives. The items can be goods people want or chores people want to avoid. The authors give procedures that keep several fairness standards satisfied at once, and for chores they show some limits on how well those standards can be met.
summary.why: Many real allocation problems, such as assigning tasks or resources as they come in, work this way, so guarantees that hold at every step matter. The text gives tight bounds (the goods result for maximin share is stated as optimal, and the chores bounds are shown optimal for some cases), which makes the results more than just an algorithm; how these results apply outside the abstract model is not addressed in the text.

papers.abstract: We study temporal fair division of indivisible items in both the goods and chores settings, with $n \ge 2$ agents and nonnegative additive values or costs. Items arrive one at a time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably. The arrival order and all agents' values or costs are known in advance, and the cumulative allocation must satisfy the fairness requirements after each arrival. For goods, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact temporal proportionality up to one item (TPROP1), a $1/n$ approximation to temporal maximin share (TMMS), and a $1/(n-1)$ approximation to temporal envy-freeness up to one item (TEF1). The TMMS factor is optimal. For chores, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact TPROP1 and a $2-1/n$ approximation to TMMS. Classical scheduling lower bounds based on fixed sequences carry over to chores TMMS, establishing the optimality of this factor for $n=2,3$. For every $n \ge 2$, we further show that $2-1/n$ is the optimal TMMS factor subject to exact TPROP1. For every fixed $n \ge 3$ and every finite $β\ge 1$, we construct an instance of chores admitting no $β$-TEF1 allocation.

papers.title: The Optimal Competitive Ratio for Subadditive Online Combinatorial Auctions is Less Than 1/2
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24920v1

summary.background:
- Combinatorial auction: a sale where buyers bid on bundles of items, not single items.
- Online: decisions must be made as each buyer arrives, without knowing future buyers.
- Competitive ratio: the worst-case fraction of the best possible (offline, all-knowing) value that an online rule guarantees.
- Subadditive valuation: a buyer's value for a bundle is at most the sum of its values for the separate items, so bundles have diminishing extra worth.
- Independent valuations: each buyer's values are drawn without depending on the others.
- Expected welfare: the average total value delivered to buyers under random values.
- Lower bound by construction: showing a ratio is impossible by exhibiting a hard instance.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds a four-buyer online combinatorial auction with independent subadditive valuations and a fixed arrival order, showing that no online allocation rule can guarantee half of the expected offline optimum, and that a 1/2 guarantee holds when there are at most three buyers.
summary.plain: This paper looks at a selling problem where buyers arrive one at a time and each must be given items immediately, without knowing who comes later. The authors build a specific example with four buyers and show that every possible online selling rule ends up with strictly less than half of the best total value an all-knowing seller could have achieved. They also state that the half-value target does hold when there are at most three buyers.
summary.why: It sharpens a known limit in online auction design by showing the best achievable guarantee is below one half for this setting, which matters for anyone hoping for a simple benchmark. The text does not say how this relates to wider applications, so its broader significance is uncertain from the abstract alone.

papers.abstract: We construct a four-buyer online combinatorial auction with independent subadditive valuations and a fixed, known arrival order in which every online rule earns strictly less than $1/2$ of the expected offline optimum. A common partition, revealed at the third arrival, gives the first three buyers one unit of welfare per item. If the rule uses three distinct partitions, either an item allocated early contributes zero or the fourth buyer's expected value for the remaining bundle is one less than its size. We compute the optimal online and offline welfare exactly and show that a $1/2$ guarantee always holds with at most three buyers.

papers.title: Exploiting Aggregate Feedback for Decentralized Equilibrium Learning in Markov Games: A Smart Grid Application
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22762v1

summary.background:
- Markov game: a repeated multi-player game where the situation (state) changes over time based on everyone's actions.
- Equilibrium (CCE / CE): a set of strategies where no player gains by unilaterally deviating; a coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) and correlated equilibrium (CE) are two standard versions, with CE being the stronger notion.
- Regret: how much worse an agent does than the best fixed strategy in hindsight; low regret bounds mean learning converges efficiently.
- Bandit feedback: the learner only sees the reward of the action it chose, not of the alternatives.
- Aggregate feedback: observing a summary (like a total or average) of all players' actions.
- Exp3-IX: a known algorithm for learning under bandit feedback with an added bias-reduction step.
- Smart grid / prosumer: households that both consume and produce energy, often with storage and demand-response programs.
- Epsilon (ε): the small allowed gap from perfect equilibrium; the sample cost scales as 1/ε².
summary.one_liner: A decentralized V-learning method for Markov games with aggregative rewards, using hybrid bandit and aggregate-predictive feedback (Exp3-IX), with a regret bound, CCE/CE learning guarantees, and a smart-grid microgrid evaluation.
summary.plain: The paper studies how several self-interested decision-makers, such as households with solar panels sharing a battery, can each learn a stable way to act when their payoff depends mostly on the combined behaviour of everyone else. Standard learning methods usually only see the reward of the action they actually took. The authors design a method that also uses the group-level totals it can observe, which they report makes learning more informative, and they test it in a simulated microgrid.
summary.why: Many real systems, such as energy markets, traffic, and pricing, have payoffs that depend on aggregates, so using aggregate signals could matter there. The text reports theoretical guarantees and simulation comparisons against three baselines, but the evidence is limited to a single simulated microgrid setting, so its practical impact is not yet established.

papers.abstract: In many multi-agent systems, an agent's payoff depends on its own action and an aggregate of other agents' actions, rather than their individual decisions. This paper investigates decentralized equilibrium learning in Markov games (MGs) with such aggregative reward structures. However, existing decentralized learning algorithms for general MGs typically rely on bandit feedback, without exploiting the additional information available from aggregate observations. To exploit this information, we develop an aggregation-predictive stage-based V-learning algorithm with hybrid-feedback Exp3-IX. Using known local reward functions and observed aggregate quantities, each agent evaluates the immediate rewards of all candidate actions and predicts their immediate losses from historical aggregate feedback, while continuation values are learned from selected-action state transitions. The algorithm requires neither opponents' individual information nor knowledge of the transition kernel. We establish a high-probability regret bound that explicitly depends on aggregate prediction errors and retains the standard worst-case order. Under a regularity condition on adaptive stage lengths, the algorithm learns an $ε$-approximate coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) within $\widetilde O(SA_{\max}T^5/ε^2)$ episodes and extends to correlated equilibrium (CE) learning. We further apply the algorithm to a renewable-rich microgrid with strategic prosumers and shared energy storage. Numerical results show smaller deviation gaps and lower gap-AUC than three learning baselines. Compared with representative demand-response rules, the learned policies exhibit weaker incentives for unilateral deviations while maintaining favorable user rewards, high renewable utilization, and relatively stable electricity prices.

papers.title: Two is better than one: optimizing binary rating scales for online platforms
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23626v1

summary.background:
- Binary feedback: each user answers a yes/no style question (a rating scale reduced to two outcomes).
- Rating scale as a threshold: a question can be modeled as a step function that says "yes" when an item's underlying quality exceeds a cutoff.
- Ranking items: the goal is to order items by their true quality based on the aggregated responses.
- Multiple scales: different users see different cutoffs, so the pooled answers carry more information.
- Adaptive design: later users' questions can depend on how earlier users responded.
- Exponential gain: the improvement in distinguishing power grows exponentially, not just linearly, with the number of rounds or scales (as stated in the text).
summary.one_liner: The paper studies how platforms should design multiple binary rating scales (with thresholds spread evenly) for different users, showing that splitting one scale into two improves item rankings and that adaptively chosen scales can give exponentially better distinguishing power.
summary.plain: Online platforms like review sites often get ratings that are inflated and tell them little, partly because of how the question is worded. This paper asks whether giving different users different rating questions, each with a yes-or-no style answer, can help separate good items from mediocre ones. The authors prove that splitting one rating scale into two can always help rankings, and that using several scales, chosen adaptively based on earlier responses, can be far more informative.
summary.why: Better rating design affects which products, hotels or videos users see first, so the question matters for platforms and their users. The text is purely theoretical and gives no empirical tests on real platforms, so its practical impact is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Online platforms often struggle with inflated, uninformative user ratings. This issue can be mitigated by better design of the data collection mechanism, for example through changing the phrasing of user questions. Previous work optimizes a single rating scale to best distinguish the inherent qualities of items under binary feedback. In this paper, we demonstrate the power of utilizing different rating scales for different users. First, we show that a designer can always split a single rating scale into two to improve item rankings. Next, we formally characterize the optimal design of multiple scales as a series of 0-1 step functions whose threshold values are evenly spaced. Finally, we consider an adaptive model where subsequent rating scales can depend on the responses from previous users and items are ranked by their full sequence of responses, and show that adaptivity leads to exponentially greater distinguishing power. All in all, our theoretical results show that using multiple rating scales significantly improves item rankings on platforms.

papers.title: Mechanism Design and Active Systems Theory: 60 Years of Parallel Development
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21803v1

summary.background:
- Mechanism design: building rules (auctions, contracts, voting, planning procedures) so that people who pursue their own interests still produce a desired outcome.
- Revelation principle: a standard result saying that one can restrict attention to rules where participants simply report their private information honestly.
- Incentive compatibility: a rule is designed so that telling the truth is in each participant's own interest.
- Contract theory: how a principal pays an agent when effort or information is hidden or hard to observe.
- Implementation theory: whether a designer can get a desired outcome as the equilibrium of some game.
- Active systems theory: a framework, developed from work by V.N. Burkov, that studies control of organizations where participants have their own goals and information.
- Robust and dynamic design: rules that still work when assumptions are wrong or when interaction unfolds over time.
summary.one_liner: A survey that compares mechanism design, contract theory and implementation theory with the Russian-origin theory of active systems and its successor, the theory of control in organizations, covering results from 2006 to 2026 and mapping where the two traditions agree and diverge.
summary.plain: This is a review paper about how to design the rules of a game or organization so that self-interested people act in a way that serves the designer's goals. It sets two research traditions side by side: the widely known Western mechanism design field and a separate Russian-led line of work called active systems theory. The authors say they match up classic results from both and point out topics that only the second tradition covers, such as staff, organizational structure and participants' beliefs.
summary.why: It is useful as a map for researchers who know only one of these two bodies of work, and it may help link ideas on incentives, contracts and AI agents across the two. The text itself gives no outside evidence of impact, so its practical importance is unclear from the abstract alone.

papers.abstract: The survey compares two research traditions within the mathematical theory of designing the rules of interaction (mechanisms) for purposeful participants: mechanism design, together with contract theory and implementation theory, and the theory of active systems created by V.N. Burkov and developed into the theory of control in organizations (TCO) by D.A. Novikov's school; the main results of Yu.B. Germeier's school and of the domestic schools adjacent to active systems theory (AST) are covered as well. The problem statements and principal results of 2006-2026 are presented: for mechanism design (MD) - robust and dynamic mechanism design, multidimensional screening, information design, simplicity of mechanisms and credibility of the designer, market design, algorithmic and learning-based design, mechanisms for AI agents, and robust, relational, dynamic and algorithmic contracts; for AST and TCO - a general typology of control, strategy-proof and incentive-compatible planning mechanisms, decomposition of the agents' game, systems with distributed control and coalitional interaction, reflexive games and informational control, control of staff and structure, dynamic active systems, and project management. A correspondence between the classical results is established (the fair play principle and the revelation principle, the serial resource allocation mechanism and the uniform rule, active expertise mechanisms and generalized median schemes, quasi-compensatory incentive schemes and contracts under observable actions), and priorities are delineated by uniform rules; the areas where the two traditions diverge are identified, as are the dimensions of the problem (staff, structure, institutions, awareness, agents' beliefs) covered only by TCO.

papers.title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for Constant-Factor EFX Allocations of Chores
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21387v1

summary.background:
- Fair division: splitting items among agents so each feels their share is fair; "chores" are items people want to avoid, so agents have disutility (cost) rather than value.
- Additive disutilities: each agent's total cost is the sum of the costs of the chores they receive.
- EFX (envy-freeness up to any item): no agent prefers another's bundle after removing any single chore from it. A multiplicative approximation relaxes this by a constant factor.
- Polynomial time: the running time grows at most like a fixed power of the input size, which is the usual meaning of "efficient" in algorithms.
- FPTAS: a method that gets arbitrarily close to an optimal answer with running time polynomial in both input size and 1/ε.
- Equilibrium with earning limits: a market-style balance where agents earn payouts for chores and money flows are constrained; the paper uses such equilibria as a starting point.
- Mirror ascent: an iterative optimization method for maximizing a function over a constrained set.
- Local maximum of a nonconvex program: a point better than all nearby points, which may not be the global best; the paper proves such points are exact equilibria.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives the first polynomial-time algorithm that computes a (3+ε)-approximate EFX allocation of indivisible chores to agents with additive disutilities, via an FPTAS for earning-restricted equilibria and a new conversion procedure feeding into the Garg–Murhekar chore-swap framework.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to divide a set of indivisible tasks ("chores") among several people so that nobody feels treated unfairly. Earlier work showed that roughly fair divisions always exist, but no efficient method was known to find one. The authors give a procedure that finds a division that is fair up to a factor of 3 plus a small tunable slack, in running time that grows polynomially with the problem size and with how small the slack is.
summary.why: Fair division of chores is a core question in algorithmic economics, and turning an existence result into an efficient algorithm is a standard and meaningful step. The authors also suggest their techniques may carry over to goods and other fairness notions, though the text does not show that.

papers.abstract: We study the fair division of indivisible chores among agents with additive disutilities, focusing on the central fairness notion of envy-freeness up to any chore (EFX), and its multiplicative approximations. Although the existence of constant-factor approximations to EFX are known, computing such an allocation in polynomial time remained open. We resolve this question by giving an algorithm that, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, computes a $(3+\varepsilon)$-EFX allocation in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$. Our result relies on two algorithmic contributions. First, we give a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for earning-restricted (ER) equilibria with equal earning requirements and arbitrary feasible chore earning limits. We develop a new nonconvex program with chore payouts and money-flow variables, and prove that every local maximum yields an exact ER equilibrium. We then give a mirror-ascent algorithm for this program and prove that it converges to an approximate ER equilibrium in polynomial time. Second, we give a new procedure that converts the approximate equilibrium into a $(3+\varepsilon)$-EFX-friendly allocation, a suitable starting point for the chore-swap framework of Garg and Murhekar (2026). The procedure uses a flexible price threshold to choose swap chores and their recipients together, overcoming a factor-four bottleneck in the earlier approaches while accommodating approximate earnings. We expect these ideas to be useful more broadly in fair division, including for goods and other fairness notions.
